In 2007, Firestone carried out the following high resolution ground geophysics surveys over the BK11
rows: In 2007, Firestone carried out the following high resolution ground geophysics surveys
over the BK11 kimberlite pipe (exact equipment type unknown):
1. Ground magnetic survey: 25m line spacing, 20m reading stations.
2. Ground Gravity Survey: 20m line spacing, 10m reading stations.
3. Ground EM survey: 25m line spacing, 10m reading stations.
That same year Firestone announced (Press Release, 30 July 2007) that the surface
size of the BK11 kimberlite was 8 Ha (an increase from the De Beers 6.5 Ha estimate).
However, in 2009, MPH Consulting Limited announced a surface size of 9.6 Ha for the
BK11 kimberlite that was used in their Feasibility Study (2009). In both cases, although
not stated, it is likely that these sizes were modelled from the high-resolution geophysics
Due to the variations in surface area (footprint), and that 9.6 Ha has been used by both
MPH Consulting Limited (2009) and Obsidian (2015) in their modelling of the BK11
kimberlite, Tango requested that the geophysical data be re-modelled to verify the size
assumptions. In July 2015, New Era Geophysics (Private) Limited (“New Era”) re-
modelled the surface size of BK11 and the shape and size with depth using 3-D
modelling techniques. New Era’s geophysicist Gavin Selfe, an ex-De Beers
geophysicist, with over 20 years of kimberlite modelling experience, quality controlled
(QC’d) the raw data and conducted the remodelling exercise.
In terms of geophysics, modelling the BK11 kimberlite pipe is complicated. Gravity will

headers: are capable of identifying the low density and conductive sediments on the margins of the crater. Th
rows: are capable of identifying the low density and conductive sediments on the margins of
the crater. The magnetic response in these marginal deposits is virtually zero although
the deeper kimberlitic material is recognised in this technique. 3D inversion modelling
was undertaken on both the magnetics and the gravity data, but the gravity model is
considered to have yielded the best results and thus has been used to calculate surface
area and the depth profile down to several hundred metres below ground surface.

• Associated minerals: potassium feldspar, biotite, and magnetite with minor quartz, apatite,

• Sodic-calcic alteration is spatially restricted to the immediate periphery of the preserved

the 2005 FS. Since that time, a number of new operations have commenced.
Suitably qualified engineers will be used for any revised design work for the HPAL
system. Similarly, RIP technology has successfully been implemented since the
1950s on over 30 full-scale operations to recover a range of metals. In the laterite
context, Clean TeQ has spent over 13 years developing and piloting the technology
on laterite ores for optimal recovery of nickel, cobalt and scandium.
• To minimise technical risks, a well-resourced owner’s management team with high
levels of expertise gained from direct exposure to developed lateritic nickel projects,
will be established. The resource and mining risk relating to the Project is deemed
to be low because of the continuity of the deposit and the use of well-established
resource estimation techniques. Resource and mining reserve estimates
established for the first generation HPAL projects have proven to be reliable.
• Land access/ acquisition agreements will need to be finalised to cover parts of the
Project area, limestone quarry, rail siding and natural gas pipeline. Additionally, the
current water allocation will need to be increased or additional licences purchased
to secure finalise the Project’s water requirements. The water requirements are yet
to be finalised and the final water access agreements are yet to be confirmed.

rows: Core was sawn in half and sampled at 2 m intervals, regardless of geology. Each sample
consisted of 2 m composites of half core, with the exception of the first and last intervals
All strongly altered or epithermal-mineralized intervals of core were sampled, with the
exception of some intervals within the Suárez Formation once it was established that this
material did not contain potentially economic levels of gold. Sampling always began at
least five samples above the start of mineralization typically encompassing the basal
10 m to 20 m of the Suárez Formation.
Sample intervals were selected using the following criteria:
• Maximum sample length of 2 m in un-mineralized lithologies
• Maximum sample length of 1 m in mineralized lithologies
• Smaller samples may be selected around high grade, visible gold-bearing veins
• Geological changes in the core such as major mineralization / alteration intensity
and lithology changes were used as sample breaks
• Core size changes and any zones of core loss were used as sample breaks
• Large discrete veins that might possibly be modelled or mined as separate
• The begin / end marks were placed so that the entire vein was included in the
